newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary energy prices worry investors - consultancy.
newsitem.headline: Hungary energy prices worry investors - consultancy.

text.p: Western investors in Hungary's energy industries may review their plans of developments in the country if Hungary fails to ensure an eight percent profit margin for the sector, a consultancy group said on Wednesday.
"Foreign investors are nervous. They do expect that the contracts signed will be kept," Wolfgang Sietz, co-owner of Eurocorpcommerz Rt, told a news conference.
"I think the government have understood that it has to keep to contracts," he added. "Otherwise investors may seriously address the question if they will invest further or not."

Sietz, whose company is consultant to Germany's RWE, owner of stakes in two electricity distributors and the Matra power station, said Hungary is making efforts to announce in November the rate of an energy price rise due on January 1.

Hungary sold large stakes in its energy distribution companies and power stations to western investors in December 1995, and promised the investors, who plan to spend billions more dollars for modernisation, to ensure an eight percent profit margin in the sector from 1997. @

The government said in August it was postponing a price rise, previously announced for October 1, as a study by the National Energy Office (MEH) had not produced all the information needed for a decision.
The government did not say how big a rise MEH had planned, but press reports said it was between 30 and 40 percent.
A government commissioner, appointed to work out a new proposal about the energy price rise due on January 1, began talks with foreign investors earlier this month. @

Sietz said foreign investors understood that the energy price rise was a political question in Hungary, where inflation was high and real wages slumped in the past two years, but they insisted on further negotiations with the government.

He said the government's latest proposals of a maximum 25 percent price rise could be acceptable to the investors, but much depended on the calculation of costs of the energy companies and of the base of the eight percent profit margin.
